title: Jukai and Susho Rituals
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett emphasized that true spiritual growth and understanding can only be achieved through a deep commitment to one's own practice, rather than seeking external validation or recognition within the community. They encouraged students to focus on skillfulness and dedication in their daily sitting meditation and other activities, rather than comparing themselves to others or striving for special status. By doing so, individuals can cultivate a sense of belonging and connection with others while also staying true to their own unique path.

sentences.text: So I'm not surprised that I didn't have a lot of time to prepare a brilliant dharma talk after all that we've been doing these last six or eight weeks.
But it says on the schedule the second Wednesday of the month is dharma talk.
So I was remembering that there's a great virtue to just sticking to the schedule.
Whether you feel ready for it, or organized, or like you have your stuff together, there's a great virtue to just the practice of showing up, not stupidly or something like that.
But we have a little fear of being wooden or too habit-bound, which leads us to be endlessly adjusting, and tweaking, and improving, and modifying, and optimizing.
A lot of verbs for this.
So I thought I would try not to do that and just try to say a few words, and if I ran out of stuff to say, you can say a few words, and if you ran out of stuff to say, I'll just go home.
Can't go too far around.
A little bit would be nice, thank you.
But firstly I want to note and celebrate that Chris fixed you up.
A moment of silence for Tibet.
Today is the 54th anniversary of Tibetan National Uprising Day.
The Chinese invaded Tibet in the early 50s.
I forgot to note which year.

And the Dalai Lama and the Tibetan theocratic government stayed in Lhasa for the first several years, like five or six or eight years they stayed in place, and tried to kind of work it out with the Chinese.
And then finally on May 10, 1959, there was a big uprising, and in the chaos of that the Dalai Lama and his advisors left on horseback, foot by foot, and have not been able to be in Tibet ever since.
And so I guess every year on May, on March 10, Tibetan National Uprising Day, the Dalai Lama gives a statement, like the State of the Union address.
And so I thought of reading it to you, but it's pretty long and not that interesting.
But just to note that our Tibetan comrades are today remembering the loss of their country.
And so it's good to have memorial days to remember what's happening.
And of course the Tibetans are only one of many, many, many groups in the world who are oppressed in some way.
So I didn't know about that until this year.
I just ran into it through some chain of events that happens when you start your inbox, and you're trying to work it out somewhere else.
I think I probably got an email from a Tibetan advocacy group.
So that was the first thing.
And the second thing was I wanted to say a few words about the big ceremonies that we did over the weekend, because not all of us were able to be there, I know.
And they're mentioned in the email and the website and all this, or maybe you didn't even notice, which is okay too.
So, the two ceremonies we did.
One is a little bit hard to translate into English, so it gets called different things.
This was a ceremony in which four people in the community did a kind of empowerment step, created and received these bib-like things that Kate's trying to learn how to wear.
It takes a while, like anything.
And in preparation for the ceremony they studied for many months, or years in some cases.
The Bodhisattva precepts are more than just memorizing a list of words.
They use these rules or guidelines to try to study their life, study their context, study their conduct, excuse me.
And so sometimes the ceremony is called jukai, which means to receive the precepts in Japanese.
Sometimes it's called zaikei tokudo, which means staying at home and receiving the way,
staying at home and receiving the way, or living the way, which is in contrast to the priest ordination, which is called zaikei tokudo, which means leaving home, leaving home and receiving the way.
But confusingly, in our particular school of Buddhism, the priests don't really leave home, so it's a little bit of an interesting difference.
Some do and some don't, but I didn't.
I did the zaikei tokudo ceremony 10 years ago, and not that much on the surface really changed.
In other Buddhist orders, full ordination means living by a lot more rules, including celibacy and not having possessions,
and living in a completely dependent relationship with the lay supporters.

And so Americans then sort of do the history in Japan, and just something about the Japanese sensibility about things, that part was released, and just the more relativistic bodhisattva precepts remained for the priests.
But the precepts that I took as a priest were the exact same precepts that these four took.
And so they're understood to be endlessly deep.
You keep studying and keep moving deeper and deeper and more dynamically and creatively into these precepts for the rest of your life.
And the other part of this ceremony that the four of them did, jukai, I guess is probably the best name.
Sometimes it also gets called in English lay ordination, which is very oxymoronic and confusing, but also accurate in its way, right?
It's an ordination and you don't become clergy.
You remain a lay person.
But the other part of it is that it also has an element of formalizing and affirming a warm relationship between you and the teacher from whom you receive this ceremony and this empowerment.
But then there are rules about who can be the giver of these precepts.
And so in the [unclear: "art situation"], Norman Fischer, our guiding teacher, has enough empowerment himself to do this, whereas I don't and Nancy doesn't.
And so we did it together, with Norman doing the official ceremonial stuff and then Nancy and myself participating and also helping to prepare the four students.
And so, like any formal step, it seems to be both tremendously helpful and a big problem.
And the tremendous help seems to constellate around some obvious factors.
One is just commitment and effort.
It's a big project.
You have to learn how to sew this thing, and not uncommonly people have to start over more than once; that has happened in this case.
And at the very beginning you have to get up enough [unclear: "witspo"] to ask a teacher if you can do it, because it's something where usually the student initiates.
Sometimes you're invited, but usually a student initiates.
You have to [unclear: "say good night"].
And you have to know about it, to ask about it.
And so there are quite a few small barriers that you have to work with.
And the study of the precepts takes a while depending on how you do it.
Sometimes there are many meetings with a teacher or a group.
And so there's an obvious benefit from just having a project, right?
And we're project-based human beings.
And if we have a religious project, a practice project, then we practice more.
You know what I mean?
It's pretty straightforward.
And so that helps us, because there's a way that Zen practice is quite, even though very formal, the root is formless.
So it's strange.
It's a very formalized practice sitting on formless roots.
And so one can just come to the Zen center week after week, day after day, year after year, and essentially do the same practice.
And that's great.
But that can also, at times, have a drifty, vague sense of, yeah, I go there and it's kind of nice, but I don't know what I'm doing.
And so having a project gets us in line, right?
So that's an obvious benefit.
Another obvious benefit, which happened very strongly in this case, is that it's usually a group ceremony.
And so there's a small group of you that are preparing for this, trying to figure out together how to do the things you have to do and talking together about the study that you have to do.
And sometimes that group [unclear: "of, or needs,"] becomes quite close.
And you end up feeling like family, and we use family language too.
We say that when you do this ceremony, you become a child of Buddha.
It says that in the ceremony, you become a child of Buddha.
And so in this case, quadruplets were born.
And so you feel very close to your Dharma sisters and brothers, right?
Who, from now on, are your Dharma sisters and brothers.
And then, of course, you map various positive and negative family dynamics on top of that to some extent.
But that's great, because in this context, it's much easier to work with.
Because for one thing, it's obviously made up, right?
They're not actually sisters and brothers.
But they are.
And so if you have expectations that aren't met in that relationship, it's not that impossible to notice.
Like, oh, I'm generating expectations.
I expect so-and-so, because you did the ceremony five years ago, to call me back and she didn't.
And that's really fucked up, and I see that I'm upset, and so on.
That's another obvious benefit: there's this group of [unclear: "Ordinese"] that moves through.
And a third benefit, which is more mysterious, is just like a wedding ceremony or any ceremony where there's preparation,
there's a container, there's a way you do it, there's the weight of tradition behind it, the ceremony itself has a certain magic.
Something happens, don't you think?
Yeah, something happens, even though I email them the text of the ceremony, right?
It's not like a super mystery, like, oh, I can't believe what they said.

They knew what was going to be said, at least they knew the words, but in a way they didn't know what was going to be said, because something happens, some magic happens, through intentionality, focus, and just shared experience in this ceremony itself.
And so a wedding is really a good analogy, because you could be with somebody
and be very close and be living together for years and years, and I've married couples like this, and you're fine, but you decide to get married and then something changes, something happens.
It's the same you, right?
Or is it?
So those are some of the benefits of the ceremony.
But then some of the problems: the most obvious problem is that the great power of Zen practice seems to be largely held by the fact that it's a community practice.
It's always constellating in community.
You can have periods of practice where you're practicing mostly alone, and the total number of hours on the cushion might, in our case, in this town and with our jobs,
be mostly at home.
But I've never met anybody who really felt like a true practitioner who could just go off and do this on their own.
You can't do this on your own, it seems like.
There are other practices you can do on your own, but Zen is very much a community-based practice, and it has a particularly, well, like I said, it has a formless root.
So we say in Zen that it's the same practice at the beginning, the same at the middle, and the same at the end.
And the instructions that we give to somebody when they first walk in here and have a 20-minute orientation are instructions that you can continue practicing for the rest of your life.
No problem.
And so, for all of us to be comfortable in this community, we to some extent need to feel some sense of belonging
and some sense of being honored and valued, because it's really hard for us to participate in a group for a long time if we don't feel those things.
We feel like we're a second-class citizen or not really that good at it, and those other guys are the good ones, and maybe I'll get good one day, or maybe I won't, or maybe I'll just serve them.
Thoughts like that arise and lead to unsustainable inner conditions.
And so, if you enter a group where it seems like there are some who have special insignia on, special rank, like the military, it can set up those kinds of dynamics.
And so now we have four more people with special insignia, right?
And so one could think, well, when do I get mine?
Which is not unreasonable, right?
It's important, it appears.
I mean, the community invested a lot of effort in these four, so am I in the next four?
Where do I sign up?
So that's one problem.
Or I am completely opposed to all insignia and ranks and people lording it over other people, and so I thought that this was a formless and egalitarian community, but darn it, I was wrong.
So I can't stay.
And that happens.
Not that long after I ordained,
some people left the community, for many reasons, but that was one factor, those kinds of things.
And so I think we are practicing in a particular lineage tradition, and it comes to us with particular traditional practices and tools, and so it's up to us to use them well.

It would not be, I think, very smart to say, steps and stages and levels and insignia and special clothes cause a lot of trouble, let's forget about all that, which some Zen teachers actually have, in fact, in America.
That's not what we're doing here in the Red Cedars Zen community, and it's not what Norman is doing with his Every Day Zen foundation, because there's just too much baby in that bathwater.
There really is.
It's a really powerful force for healing, to take on these practices when they're right for you, and very transformational.
You would think so in a little bit, but studying would not be transformational, necessarily.
It really can be if it's right for you.

So where it falls to us is to be committed to skillfulness in our employment of these traditional forms, and so to have talks exactly like this, explaining that we still love you if you don't get the special thing ever.
You're fully a member of the community, as much as anybody else.

And also for all of us, in the way that we understand our own practice and work with our own mind on a moment-by-moment basis, as we inevitably find judgment and clinging and comparison arising, we are all committed to working with that.
And then the more empowerment you get, the more opportunity you have to work, right?

As a community, we're committed to understanding both of these sides, and so loving Karen and Kate and Marty and Terry all the more, and appreciating them and being grateful to them for taking this step, loving everyone else just the same, just the same.
So that's a little bit about Jukai.
There's more information about this on the website you can read, and there's more and more stuff on Buddhism, which most of it seems to be really quite accurate on Wikipedia.
So I recommend Wikipedia, you could look all this up on Wikipedia.
One thing I found out on Wikipedia that I didn't know, and this is, I guess, speculative, is that nobody really knows where the actual garment came from, for sure.
Chris can correct me if I got this screwed around, but even Gene Selkirk's book didn't really seem to say.

On Wikipedia it says that they believe that during one of several periods of oppression of Buddhism in China (our whole form came from China, right, so the robes, the big [unclear: "gong"] sleeves and stuff, those are Chinese robes), during a time of oppression in China, it might be that they created this robe so they could wear it under their clothes.
During the repressions they would force everyone to defrock and disrobe, and no clergy, and burn the temples down and stuff like that.

So it might be that Buddhist clergy figured out a robe, a Buddhist robe that they could hide, and then that tradition died out in China but was kept up in Japan and used in a different way in Japan than had been used in China.
So maybe that's where it came from.
Maybe it also has, in addition to having a sense of being clothed in Buddhist clothing, also a sense of past suffering and oppression, and survival of oppression.
Maybe that's a little bit in there too, just like Tibet.
So that's what we seem to most be calling Jukai, receiving the precepts.
There's a whole other version of Jukai in Japan that's different, but we'll get into that.
We did that on Sunday afternoon.
This is like our biggest ceremony day in history.
We did that on Sunday afternoon, and then Sunday morning we did different ceremonies, and I want to talk about that a little bit also.
Those come later in one's Zen career, after this Jukai ceremony, which is a pretty wide funnel.
Any number of people might do Jukai, and it's typically done after three or four or five years of practice, something like that, or longer, but usually not in the first year or two.
If somebody asks, we usually say, why don't you keep practicing, and we'll muse about whether it makes sense for you to do this Jukai ceremony.
Jukai also has a sense of commitment to practice, but it's not a rigid commitment.
Receiving Jukai doesn't mean that you've got to sit [unclear: "thousand"] every day for the rest of your life.
Circumstances might change, it might not make sense for you anymore to practice in this particular way.
But it definitely has a sense of, I'm really in harmony with this way of practice, and it helps my heart, and I want to enter more fully into that.
So you don't want to do something like that too hastily, because you'll feel bad if you turn out to be like...
So then, somewhat later, comes the next ceremony.
It was originally a training step for priests, but it's been adapted so there could be priests or lay people now, the way we're doing it.
This is the practice of being head student, which Bob just completed.
It's kind of a teacher empowerment, but it doesn't necessarily mean one's going to be formally a Dharma teacher.
It's just like any other ordination, it's a kind of ordination, where it has all those same elements of commitment, deepening, the magic of ritual, and community.
And this one's very obviously community.

So the way they figured out to train Zen teachers (this is really smart, I think, of our Zen ancestors, and I'm not sure if they really do it this way in Japan now, but maybe we'll find out) was that the only way you could really be a teacher is if you embody a certain role within a community.
You don't go off to teacher training school and learn 50 techniques, and then do a little internship at the end, like they do with elementary school teachers.
Bad plan.
I guess it works for some people.
Instead they say, okay, the only way you could really be a teacher is if you could function as the center.
Zen teaching is not about imparting information exactly, right?
It's about being able to function in a certain way and hold the space in a certain way for a community.
The way that they figured out to do this is we'll have this position of head monk.
The head monk would serve during a time of intensive practice, with a [unclear: "nasty community surround them"].
During that time they would take on special roles, ceremonial roles and formal teaching roles.
That's what Bob and the four or five head students we've had before him did.
In our case, we create a six-week practice period and have some extra events.
It's not actually that many extra events if you look at the calendar, a couple more a week, but it's mostly a container of effort and intentionality and commitment.
The shuso commits to showing up for everything, shifting out of that, oh, should I go tonight or not go?
When you're shuso, you just go.
So it's taking that step of working with those levels of resistance or logistics, or whatever they are for you, towards full commitment for that period.
We have the shuso teach a class and do some other stuff.
But then the final piece, which Bob did on Sunday morning with us, is the big ceremony, where you basically enact being Buddha.
It sounds like impossible, right?
They put you up in a high seat, although we forgot to raise up his seat, but it was still a high seat.
They put you up in a high seat and all the other bodhisattvas in the audience ask you a Dharma question and you have to respond on the spot.
You can't be like, well, let me think about that.
You just have to be like, question arise, your answer; question arise, your answer.
These are not academic questions, but questions from the heart about practice.
I can't remember anymore who asked, but sometimes it's like, what do I do about, my heart is breaking, what do I do?
Somebody said something like that, I think: I'm mourning a loss, how do I practice with that?
And you just have to say something.

The strange thing about it is that in the context of being shuso, having been supported like that for six or nine or ten or twelve weeks and acting in the middle, you bend in the middle, like the hub in the middle of the wheel.

Somehow, experientially, you're gradually learning how to be more spacious and more responsive and less like your own smart or not smart self, but more like, I don't know what you say, a vessel or something like that.
You're almost by accident getting the hang of that over the practice period.

Then at the ceremony, which is usually during a sesshin, so you've been doing lots of meditation, they sit you down in a special seat, they create this very formal context with a very slow and decorous beginning, and chanting and bells and, you know what I mean?
It's just like incense smoke and everyone's saying.
Somehow you're able to take that final step a little more fully into emptiness.
And then when people ask, it's not exactly you answering.
It is you, and it isn't you.
It's more just response, and just meeting can occur.
It's quite beautiful to me.
So if you didn't make it on Sunday, hopefully we'll have more shusos and hopefully you can come, because it's a very impressive ceremony.
Then you ask the person afterwards, how did you think of all those answers?
Most of them say, I don't really remember what I said, actually.
Do you remember everything you said?
Actually, John here was the best case so far.
He was like, there's no way I'm going to do this.
Like impossible.
And of course he did.
I don't remember that.
So this ceremony, for a priest, is a second of four ordinations.
The next is followed by a Dharma transmission and then a formal ceremony for that.
But for laypeople, it seems to me, in our Americans and communities, it's an acknowledgement of a certain stage of practice and maturity and the ability to do some teaching.
But even that some teaching differs for each person and is done always in consultation with your teacher.
Sometimes after you've been shuso, you give formal Dharma talks.
Sometimes you do start doing the private interviews, practice discussion, that so far in our community John and Nancy and I have been doing.
And then sometimes you do other kinds of teacher role things.
Some people who have been shuso end up running temples and sitting groups.
Some people end up doing totally other things.
Bob here is interested in doing really long backpacking retreats, and so this shuso training should help empower him.
It has just the same as Jukai the same huge set of potential projections and problems, and great benefit and healing.
And it's not just for the person, it's the whole community.
There's a maturity that arises in the whole community.
It takes a pretty mature Dharma community for this even to function.
If the Dharma community wasn't mature and the practice period wasn't really working and you sat down to do the ceremony, it just wouldn't work, you know what I mean?
You'd be hokey and the answers would feel made up and phony.
That does actually happen, luckily it doesn't happen here.
So the shuso ceremony also has a sense of the shuso, by serving as this hub in the middle of a wheel, helping to spin the wheel, you know what I mean?
They're like the grease, or it's like a wheel with an empty hub or something.
Anyway, many analogies could work.
So anyway, that was longer than I intended, but I just wanted to say a few words about the ceremonies because it's potentially a little confusing and a little shocking.
Oftentimes people think Zen is nothing but sitting meditation, right?
And then they come and they say, well, there's a little ritual, I guess.
Okay, sitting meditation, a little ritual.
And then you hang around and you say, oh, thank God, like all this.
And then eventually it's like, oh my gosh, it's a religion.
Darn!
Or wonderful, depends on your history.
So anyway, powerful practice from tradition and I suppose religion with benefiting problems like everything else in human life.
